screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Over 100,000 years humans have gained great power, but power is not wisdom: humanity now faces ecological collapse, AI that may escape its control and the risk of a new world war. Harari asks why a species so good at gathering information and power is so poor at gaining wisdom. The Greek myth of Phaethon, son of the sun god, and the poem by Goethe, author of the cautionary tale The Sorcerer's Apprentice, warn against unleashing powers one cannot control. Yet both blame one person's hubris, while human power always comes from cooperation among many people.

So the problem is a network problem, and more precisely an information problem. Information holds networks together; single humans usually want the truth, but large networks create order by relying on fictions and mass delusions. This is why Nazism and Stalinism were among the strongest networks ever built, and why deluded networks are not doomed to fail.

The naive view of information holds that enough information brings truth, and truth brings power and wisdom. It has been the creed of the computer age, and it is sometimes right: shared medical data raised the share of children who reach 15 from about half around 1797 to 95.6% worldwide by 2020. Yet humanity has more information than ever and is nearer than ever to destroying itself. AI is the first technology that can decide and create by itself, so trusting it is a far bigger gamble than trusting an enchanted broom. Marc Andreessen, an American investor, expects AI to save the world, while leading AI experts fear a Silicon Curtain dividing rival powers, or dividing all humans from AI overlords.

The populist view, voiced by populist leaders such as Donald Trump and Jair Bolsonaro, treats information as a weapon: only power is real, so institutions that seek truth must be lying. Harari traces this line of thought to Karl Marx, who saw history as a struggle of oppressors and oppressed. The view is incoherent, and its two escapes, radical empiricism and divine revelation, erode trust in institutions or hand all power to one leader. The book takes the middle ground: information is neither a sure path to truth nor just a weapon. So it starts by asking what information is.

items.title: The network problem
items.text: Human power comes from cooperation in large networks, not from one person's hubris or greed. The way such networks are built makes them likely to use their power unwisely.

items.title: An information problem
items.text: Information holds networks together. Single humans usually want the truth, but large networks bind members and create order with fictions and delusions, so deluded networks such as Nazism and Stalinism can be very strong.

items.title: The naive view
items.text: Enough information brings truth, and truth brings power and wisdom, so the cure for error is more information. It has been the creed of the computer age; it was right about child deaths but misses humanity's drift toward self-destruction.

items.title: Wisdom
items.text: Making right decisions; but what is right depends on values that differ between people, cultures and ideologies, so the same knowledge can make a vaccine or a weapon.

items.title: The Silicon Curtain
items.text: A divide of chips and code rather than barbed wire. It may split rival powers in a new global conflict, or split all humans from new AI overlords, a totalitarian threat to everyone.

items.title: Dumb tools and AI
items.text: Knives, bombs and gramophones cannot process information, so humans decide how they are used. AI is the first technology that decides and creates by itself, and it already decides on mortgages, jobs and prison sentences.

items.title: The populist view
items.text: Treats information as a weapon: only power is real, so institutions that claim to seek truth, from judges to journalists, must be lying. Harari traces it to Karl Marx and finds it surprisingly Marxist even on the right.

items.title: Two populist solutions
items.text: Populism is incoherent, since its own leaders would also be lying for power. It escapes through radical empiricism, which trusts no institution and checks everything alone, or divine revelation, which trusts scriptures or a charismatic leader.

items.title: The middle ground
items.text: The book's stance: populists rightly distrust the naive view but wrongly think only power is real. Information is neither a sure path to truth nor just a weapon.

questions.a: Any object, a shutter, a star or a pigeon, can be information in the right context and mean nothing in another.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Many thinkers now see information as the most elementary part of reality, but the book, a work of history, looks only at the role of information in history. Information is not only symbols made by humans. Cher Ami, an army carrier pigeon, carried the message of Major Charles Whittlesey, the battalion's commander, and helped save his trapped men. Sarah Aaronsohn, a NILI commander, signalled British ships with a shutter, and a NILI pigeon that landed at an Ottoman officer's house gave the spy ring away. So any object can be information in the right context.

The naive view says objects become information when people use them to seek truth: information represents reality, and a successful representation is truth. The book accepts that truth is an accurate representation of some aspects of one universal reality, but truth and reality differ. Every account leaves aspects out, and a complete one would be reality itself, like the full-size map in a story by Jorge Luis Borges, author of the story On Exactitude in Science. Reality has an objective level, such as the date Aaronsohn died, and a subjective level, such as how Israelis and Palestinians see her; on both, truth can be told from error.

The naive view calls failed representations misinformation or disinformation and cures them with more information, as in the counterspeech doctrine linked with Louis D. Brandeis, a U.S. Supreme Court justice. Harari disagrees: astrology and the Bible erred, yet shaped history, so errors and fictions are information too. What defines information is connection: it creates new realities by tying points into networks. Music and DNA represent nothing, yet they make people move together or link trillions of cells into a body, and a failing network disintegrates rather than being misinformed.

So information sometimes represents reality and always connects. Rejecting the naive view does not mean rejecting truth or treating information as a weapon, but truthful accounts take a special, costly effort, so more and faster information tends to swamp them. Across history connectivity has grown without a matching rise in truth or wisdom, which is why Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union were not weakened by their delusions. The book turns next to the first information technology: the story.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Sapiens rule the world not because they are wise but because they alone cooperate flexibly in large numbers. Personal bonds reach only a few hundred people, which keeps chimpanzee and Neanderthal groups small. Changes in brain and language apparently let Sapiens tell and believe fictional stories, which added human-to-story chains: strangers need only know the same story, so a network such as the Catholic Church can link about 1.4 billion people.

Followers bond with a story about a leader rather than with the person: Joseph Stalin, at the centre of one of history's biggest personality cults, knew that Stalin meant his public image. A brand is such a story, and the tale of Cher Ami, the army carrier pigeon of Chapter 1, was partly one: Frank Blazich, a historian, found that headquarters knew the battalion's location before the pigeon arrived. The story of Jesus, a typical Jewish preacher, spread far beyond the man. Stories also turn strangers into family, as the Passover meal makes Jews remember the exodus as their own past.

Stories even add a third level of reality. Objective things such as an asteroid exist whatever anyone thinks, subjective things such as pain exist in one mind, and intersubjective things such as laws, gods, nations and money exist in the stories people tell one another. So stories build networks through fake memories, fictional relationships and intersubjective realities, which made Sapiens the most powerful animal. Harari argues that the Marxist view of stories as a smoke screen for material interests is wrong, because stories define the identities and interests of large groups; Germans who chose the Nazi story in 1933 made a tragic mistake.

Power needs both truth and order, and those who keep order usually command those who know the truth. Fiction has two advantages: it can be simple and it can comfort. Plato, author of the Republic, imagined a noble lie about the origin of the social order, but there is a third option: a fiction that admits it is fiction, like the U.S. Constitution, which could be amended to abolish slavery, unlike the Ten Commandments. Truth and order often conflict, so Nazi Germany could lead in rocket science while banning doubt about its racist myths. History is a tightrope walk between truth and order, and the book turns next to the written document.

items.title: Human-to-human and human-to-story chains
items.text: Networks of personal bonds stay small, because humans can bond closely with only a few hundred people. Stories add a new chain: people need not know each other, only the same story.

items.title: Brand
items.text: A story told about a product or a person that may have little to do with the real thing, as with Coca-Cola, influencers and Stalin.

items.title: Three levels of reality
items.text: Objective reality exists whether or not anyone knows it; subjective reality exists in one mind; intersubjective reality exists between many minds, in the stories they exchange, and disappears when they stop.

items.title: Three ways stories build networks
items.text: By implanting fake memories, as at Passover; by forming fictional relationships, as among Christian brothers and sisters; and by creating intersubjective realities, such as gods, nations, law codes and currencies.

items.title: Stories, not just interests
items.text: Harari argues that the Marxist view of stories as a smoke screen for material interests is wrong: stories define the identities of large groups, so large-scale identities and interests are always intersubjective.

items.title: Truth and order
items.text: Every information network must at once discover truth and create order. Power needs both, but those who keep order usually command those who know the truth.

items.title: Two advantages of fiction over truth
items.text: Fiction can be as simple as we like, while truth is as complicated as reality; and fiction can be shaped to comfort and flatter, while truth is often painful.

items.title: The noble lie
items.text: Plato's fictional story about the origin of the social order, told to make citizens loyal and stop them questioning the constitution; many states have told versions of it.

items.title: Truth, lie and the third option
items.text: A fictional story is a lie only when it pretends to represent reality truly; when it admits that it creates a new intersubjective reality, it is not a lie.

items.title: Human origin and divine origin
items.text: A fiction that admits humans made it can be amended, as the U.S. Constitution was to abolish slavery; one that claims divine origin, like the Ten Commandments, cannot be changed.

items.title: Coca-Cola
items.text: Tens of billions of dollars of advertising taught people to link a flavoured drink with fun, happiness and youth.

items.title: The Loch Ness Monster
items.text: Whether it exists is an objective question for sonar and DNA: a 2019 DNA survey found many species but no monster.

items.title: Disputed states
items.text: Kosovo, Abkhazia and the United States between 1776 and 1783 show that a state exists when enough people agree it does.

items.title: A billionaire on an island
items.text: A billionaire alone on a desert island finds his banknotes and bonds worthless, since their value lives inside a network.

items.title: Tribes and Neanderthals
items.text: Bands linked by shared stories formed tribes of hundreds or thousands, which beat isolated Neanderthal bands and spread new knowledge.

items.title: The mammoth hunters' spell
items.text: A powerless spell promising dead hunters a good afterlife gave the living courage and solidarity, so it helped the hunt.

items.title: Darwin's theory
items.text: It explains the origin of species but undermines central myths, so governments and churches have limited its teaching, giving up truth for order.

rows.name: Human-to-human chains
rows.text: Networks built from personal bonds only, so they stay small

rows.name: Human-to-story chains
rows.text: People linked through a story they all know, with no upper limit

rows.name: Brand
rows.text: A story told about a product or person, often far from the truth

rows.name: Objective reality
rows.text: Things that exist whether or not anyone is aware of them

rows.name: Subjective reality
rows.text: Things that exist in one mind's awareness of them

rows.name: Intersubjective reality
rows.text: Things that exist between many minds, created by exchanging stories

rows.name: The noble lie
rows.text: A fictional story about the origin of the social order, told to keep citizens loyal

rows.name: The third option
rows.text: A fiction that admits it creates a new intersubjective reality, so it is no lie

rows.name: Truth and order
rows.text: The two tasks of every information network: discover truth and create order

items.title: The question
items.text: Why do we Sapiens gain information and power but not wisdom?

items.title: Established so far
items.text: The prologue argued that power comes from large networks bound by fictions; Chapter 1, that information is defined by connection, not truth.

items.title: This chapter adds
items.text: Stories let strangers cooperate without limit, and because order is easier with fiction than truth, networks can grow powerful without growing wise.

items.title: Where it stops
items.text: History is a tightrope walk between truth and order; the book turns to its next information technology, the written document.

rows.name: Balancing truth and order
rows.text: How can a network balance truth with order as information speeds up?

rows.name: The written document
rows.text: How will written documents, the next technology, test the balance of truth and order?

rows.name: Correcting the Constitution
rows.text: How did the U.S. Constitution correct its own injustices, as Chapter 5 will show?
